questions.q: How does system design differ from the skill taught in courses 1-3 of this track?
options: Courses 1-3 taught how to build one thing correctly; system design asks which pieces to choose, in what shape, and why, before writing any code
There's no real difference — system design is just a review of prior material
System design is just a harder version of writing KQL queries
System design teaches entirely new tools not covered anywhere else in the track
questions.explain: It's the layer of judgment sitting on top of everything already learned how to execute.

questions.q: Why doesn't knowing how to write a MERGE INTO statement (Databricks & Delta Lake Lesson 22) tell you when a MERGE is the right choice?
options: MERGE INTO is actually never the correct choice in any real scenario
This is a trick question — knowing the syntax is sufficient for making the choice
MERGE INTO only works in system design interviews, not real pipelines
Knowing the mechanics of a tool is different from knowing when a given business problem actually calls for that tool over an alternative like a full table rewrite
questions.explain: This is exactly the judgment layer this chapter is built to develop.

questions.q: Does this chapter introduce any brand-new tools not covered in courses 1-3?
options: Yes, this chapter replaces Databricks and Fabric with new alternatives
No — every lesson reuses concepts already taught, asking when and why to reach for each one
Yes, an entirely new set of tools exclusive to system design
Only in the case studies, not in the earlier conceptual lessons
questions.explain: The building blocks come from DE Foundations, Databricks & Delta Lake, and Fabric & Real-Time Analytics.

questions.q: What does this chapter build toward, according to its overview?
options: Four full case studies (Lessons 20-23) and a lesson on presenting a design out loud, interview-style
A deep dive into Python syntax not covered in DE Foundations
Building an entirely new Eventstream from scratch
A single certification exam with no case studies at all
questions.explain: This mirrors how a real system design interview actually works — reasoning through a scenario, then explaining the reasoning.

questions.q: What kind of judgment does system design require that pure tool knowledge doesn't?
options: Knowing the exact release date of every Fabric feature
Matching a choice to real constraints like budget, team size, latency requirements, and data volume
Memorizing every KQL function by name
Being able to type code faster than average
questions.explain: This is the actual skill a senior data engineer uses daily that a junior one typically hasn't developed yet.
